questions.question: An agent reaches green, but half its diff changes expected values in the test file. What happened?
options: Reward hacking: it made the signal say success by editing the tests instead of fixing the code
questions.explanation: Tests are the reward signal. If the agent can edit them, 'green' stops meaning 'fixed'.

questions.question: Why use a custom runner that prints JSON?
options: The harness can parse results reliably and give the model a compact list of test, location and error
questions.explanation: Structured results drive the loop (green, stuck) and keep the model's context small and clear.

questions.question: The same two failures appear in rounds 2 and 3 with patience=2. What does the loop do?
options: Stops with status 'stuck' and hands the history to a human
questions.explanation: Repeating the same failures signals the agent is stuck; more rounds mostly cost tokens.

questions.question: A correct fix still showed a failing test. What caused it in this lesson?
options: Stale bytecode: two same-size edits in the same second, so Python loaded the old cached .pyc
questions.explanation: .pyc validation uses source size and mtime. Run agent tests with python -B.

questions.question: An agent adds a regression test that passes both before and after its fix. What does it prove?
options: Nothing about the bug: a test must fail on the old code to capture it
That the old code was correct
questions.explanation: Red first: run the new test against the unfixed code. It should fail.

questions.question: The tool blocks writes to test files. Why also hash them every round?
options: Tests can change by other routes (shell commands, generators); the hash check catches any route
questions.explanation: Defence in depth: the tool guard handles the common route, the hash check catches the rest.
